chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Why today's big bands fall short of Basie and Duke
summary: Wilson argues current arrangers for Ferguson, Herman and Rich are good but none rebuilds the mass audience that Basie, Ellington and Goodman had.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Now any of these bands, as good as they are -- all these arrangements by people like Sam Nistico; and some of these arrangers that seem to be so busy now writing for Maynard Ferguson and Woodie Herman and Buddy Rich-- this stuff is absolutely good. But I just don't see it doing the job that it should do to really lift that big band thing up where the bottom fell out, after Kenton, because the best is still Count Basie -- to have a big

audience and still play good big band music. Although these other guys are good, they are not important enough, they haven't come through -- Maynard Ferguson's band or Buddy Rich's band is fine for drum leader. That's good enough, but I mean for a big band, you know, regardless of the leader, the big jazz band, to carry on where Basie and Duke left and of course, when I say Benny Goodman, that's Fletcher Henderson sound -- Fletcher Henderson originated the Goodman style, you know.

To carry on in that is something new. Because those things had a big mass public and still had fine musicians, too. Duke and -- but to carry on. I'd love to see the arrangers that Woodie is hiring now and Maynard Ferguson and these others, and stuff that I hear. I even hear in Boston, the Herb Pomeroy Band that everyone raves about, I just don't see that it's the important thing that's missing in the big band field, to bring that big public back into the big band.
